issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette: Amir sat in his cluttered studio, surrounded by half-finished sculptures and the faint scent of clay. It had been two years since the accident that shattered his life - a fall from a ladder while working on a commissioned piece, leaving him with multiple fractures and a punctured lung. As he gingerly moved his hands over his latest project, he couldn't shake off the feeling that his body was no longer reliable. "I used to be so sure of myself," he thought, "but now every little ache or pain makes me wonder if I'm on the verge of another disaster." This fear had become all-consuming, driving him to constantly monitor his body for signs of danger or injury. Amir would catch himself checking his pulse, his breathing, and even the color of his skin - anything that might signal impending doom. His family doctor had reassured him that he was making a full recovery, but Amir couldn't shake off the conviction that he had been permanently changed for the worse. He felt vulnerable, as if his body had been irreparably damaged by the accident. As a result, Amir began to avoid situations that put his body under stress - no more hiking, no more heavy lifting, and certainly no more climbing ladders. His art, once a source of joy and expression, now seemed like a liability. He found himself questioning every move, every gesture, as if one wrong step would lead to catastrophe. "What's the point of creating something beautiful if I'm just going to end up breaking myself?" he thought. Amir's studio, once a sanctuary, had become a constant reminder of his limitations. He spent more and more time thinking about why the accident had happened to him - was it punishment for some past transgression? A test of his resolve? The more he dwelled on these questions, the more lost he felt. His mind became trapped in an endless loop of "what ifs" and "maybes," each one reinforcing his conviction that his body was fragile and untrustworthy. As the days turned into weeks, Amir's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on his relationships. His friends and family grew concerned about his withdrawal, but he couldn't explain why he felt so stuck. He just knew that every time he tried to push past his fears, his body seemed to betray him - a twinge in his back, a flutter in his chest, or a wave of dizziness would send him scurrying for cover. Lately, Amir had been wondering if he'd ever be able to reclaim his life, his art, and his sense of self. The accident had left him feeling like a fragile vase, one wrong move away from shattering into a thousand pieces. As he looked around his studio, he felt a deep sadness wash over him - would he ever be able to create again, or was that part of him forever lost?
